Setting the scene

text.content: In the previous lesson, Meridian's development team added deterministic routing using the Condition Node. The routing worked well for clear status requests but Test 3 exposed a real problem: the query "What is the escalation status procedure for severity level 2 issues?" routed to the live data path because the word "status" appeared in the sentence even though the query was genuinely asking about a policy procedure, not live engagement data.

rich_text.plain_text: In the previous lesson, Meridian's development team added deterministic routing using the Condition Node. The routing worked well for clear status requests but Test 3 exposed a real problem: the query "What is the escalation status procedure for severity level 2 issues?" routed to the live data path because the word "status" appeared in the sentence even though the query was genuinely asking about a policy procedure, not live engagement data.

text.content: Klaus Brandt reviewed the test results and flagged the issue immediately. If a consultant asks about an escalation procedure and gets a placeholder response about live data lookup, the agent has failed. Not because of a technical error, but because keyword matching cannot understand intent.

rich_text.plain_text: What the Condition Agent Node does differently

text.content: The Condition Agent Node provides AI-driven dynamic branching based on natural language instructions and context. It uses a Large Language Model to route the workflow. It analyzes provided input data against a set of user-defined scenarios guided by high-level natural language instructions that define the decision-making task.

rich_text.plain_text: The Condition Agent Node provides AI-driven dynamic branching based on natural language instructions and context. It uses a Large Language Model to route the workflow. It analyzes provided input data against a set of user-defined scenarios guided by high-level natural language instructions that define the decision-making task.

text.content: The LLM then determines which scenario best fits the current input context. This node is particularly useful for tasks like user intent recognition, complex conditional routing, or nuanced situational decision-making where simple predefined rules are insufficient.

Instructions:

text.content: You are a query classifier for Meridian Consulting's internal agent. Your task is to determine whether the consultant's query is requesting live engagement status data for a specific client project, or whether it is asking about Meridian's internal policies, procedures, documentation, or general knowledge. Classify the query as "status_request" only when the consultant is explicitly asking for the current live status, progress update, or real-time information about a specific named client engagement or project. Classify the query as "knowledge_query" for everything else including questions about Meridian's internal policies, procedures, escalation rules, regional guidelines, project classification, or any other knowledge base content, even if the word "status" appears in the query in a different context.

Takeaway:

text.content: The Condition Agent Node makes routing decisions the way a human would by understanding what the consultant is trying to accomplish, not by matching words in the query.

rich_text.plain_text: The Condition Agent Node makes routing decisions the way a human would by understanding what the consultant is trying to accomplish, not by matching words in the query.

text.content: This comes at a cost: every routing decision requires a Gemini API call, which adds latency compared to the Condition Node's instant rule evaluation. The right choice between the two depends on the nature of the routing problem. When triggers are clear and unambiguous, use the Condition Node. When intent matters more than keywords, use the Condition Agent Node.
